description: 67 degrees F, 97% humidity, heavy drizzle stopped about 10 minutes prior. At 5:28 pm, walking back to my car with my cousin, I spotted this male Wood Duck in the southern end of Shoal Creek, which was separated from the Colorado River by the Ann and Roy Butler Hike and Bike Trail. The water looked more murky than usual, likely due to rainfall disturbing the silt at the bottom of the creek. The male was at first in water between a small island where two female Great-tailed grackles were fighting over something, and the overhanging foliage on the right side. There was a fisherman in the back, but he was far enough not to be a concern to the duck. He began to swim northwards up Shoal Creek, towards a Red-eared slider basking on top of storm drain, but I tried to lure it back by throwing pieces of honey wheat bread into the water. The break caught his attention, but he was very wary of either me, or of this male Great-tailed grackle that flew into the scene once I started throwing bread. The closest I could get him to come was about 10 ft from the grassy side of the bike trail where I stood, and after 10 minutes, he retreated under the hanging foliage without eating any of the bread.

description:
Wood Duck (Aix sponsa), 2 pairs, males in eclipse plumage, see notes below. Big John's Pond, Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge (East Side), Broad Channel, Queens, NY.

The first photo is cropped from the second (original) photo to show the 2 males. The second photo shows all 4 birds in the water but one of the females has been attacked (by a Snapping Turtle) and is being killed by drowning as it appears to be grasped by the turtle by its head. I had previously noticed this bird feeding in the water by dabbling but my attention was only drawn to it by the flapping of its wings and its struggles when it was attacked, which briefly pulled the predator out of the water, showing its plastron. The commotion alarmed the 2 juvenile Black-crowned Night Herons (which were perched on the tree on the left) and also brought the other 3 ducks to the vicinity of the dying bird. The male that seemed to be the mate of the attacked female approached the attacked bird and kept sounding a distress call but none of the ducks attempted to drive off the predator or rescue their companion (I realize I am perhaps anthropomorphizing the situation). Although it attempted to raise its wings feebly a few times the attacked bird appeared to die (either by drowning or by injuries from predator) fairly soon, and when I checked back at Big John's pond (after visiting the East Garden) the floating dead bird was being tugged at and moved about by the feeding actions of the turtle, which showed its dorsum and occasionally its head. The 3 ducks were later at the far side of the pond, out of the water, the 2 males together and the female apart. See next observation for Snapping Turtle.

description: We saw a pair of Wood Ducks (Aix sponsa) at the Moraine State Park Waterfowl Observation deck. The male had a crested iridescent green head with white stripes on its throat, breast, and tail. The chest was a deep speckled brown. He also had a very distinct red eye. The female is mostly dull speckled brown with a pale ring around her eye. Both the male and female have bright blue patches on their wings. There was light precipitation and a very dense fog in the area until about 10:30am. The temperature was in the 50°. Other species seen were Ruddy Ducks (Oxyura jamaicensis), Canada geese (Branta canadensis), and Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos). The Wood Duck looks a lot like the Mallard, and was hard to identify at first glance. The crest on the males head and white stripes helped identify them.

description:
White Rock lake, greater sunset bay woods
Photo story
Photo 1:
Wood Duck In A Tree
I heard noise above my head & found a male wood duck up there quacking away.  Not surprising this time of year because wood ducks nest in cavities of trees.  Not on the ground like most other ducks do.  
Photo 2:
Here Comes Mama Wood Duck
I was a bit startled when I heard a loud flapping & a female wood duck landed in the tree beside me.  
Photo 3:
House Hunting
She poked her head inside a cavity I didn't know was there.  It was obvious this couple was house hunting for a nest site.  And they had different ideas on which site was best.
Photo 4:
Papa Finds Another Hollow Branch
Now it was Papa Wood Duck's turn to fly over to a large tree beside me and find another hole.  He quacked a couple of times as though to call out to the female about this one.
Photo 5:
I Like This One Better
Mama refused to go look at Papa's nest choice and quacked back that she liked this one better.  It was getting noisy.
Photo 6:
Here Is Another One
Papa responded by flying over to yet another hollow branch.  Again he quacked to get Mama to come & check it out.  
Photo 7:
Taking A Closer Look
Mama ignored Papa and continued to check out her choice.
Photo 8:
This is the One, Honey
It appears we have a winner.
Photo 9:
But You Didn't Even Look At This One
The male sounded kind of forlorn as he continued to quack even though the female totally ignored him. 
Photo 10:
Women!!!
I took this last shot of the male looking a bit dismayed that all his suggestions had been ignored by his mate.  I thought the whole thing was pretty funny.

description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
Photo story
Photo 1:
Take the Bread & Run!
I was watching a family feed bread to a large gathering of ducks and coots.  There was a lot of pushing, shoving and bickering going on for the unhealthy but apparently tasty junk food.  Suddenly this one female wood duck snatched an entire soggy heel of bread and took off running away from the crowd in the direction of the shallow water.  
Photo 2:
Waddle Waddle Waddle
Had to laugh when she reached the shallow water.  She was awkwardly waddling as fast as she could.  Somehow the bread seemed to throw her off balance so that she was waddling a bit bow-legged.
Photo 3:
Finally, I Can Swim
When she reached deeper water, she was finally able to swim.  She was sneaky, none of the ducks on shore saw her steal the bread.  
Photo 4:
Hey Honey, Look What I Found!
Now I understand why she didn't just eat the bread like the other ducks and coots.  She was taking it to share with her mate.  
Photo 5:
Sharing With My Sweetheart
It was so sweet when he took some of the bread & they swam off together.  In summer, wood ducks are in eclipse plumage so the male looked very similar to the female, except for his bill which does not show until the next photo.
Photo 6:
It's All About the Eyes
Well, and the bill too.  Now you can tell which one is the male.  He has the red eyes and colorful bill.  Otherwise, he looks same as the female.  Nothing like the spectacular colorful feathers he has in breeding season.
Photo 7:
Bath Time
After the bread was eaten, they proceeded to splash and bathe.  A perfect ending to a romantic meal for two.  I enjoyed watching this sweet moment in their life.

description:
White Rock lake, East Lawther Drive area
Photo 1:
Can You Spot The Wood Duck?
A friend showed me a wood duck nesting site.  Giant tree with a hollow part.  I would never have seen it on my own.  With this uncropped view, can you spot the wood duck?
Photo 2:
There She Is
This one is cropped to see her better.  She is standing at the opening to this hollow part of the tree.  Wood ducks nest high in tree cavities.  
Photo 3:
Dad is On the Other Side of the Giant Tree
When I was walking around the nest tree, I discovered Dad on the opposite side, standing guard.
Photo 4:
Entrance To Her Nest
This was the best side to see her and the opening to her nest.  My friend had seen her going in and out but all she did while I was there was quack quietly as she stood there.
Only shots I got of this nest because a rat snake got whatever was inside, not sure if eggs or babies.  The friend who showed me this nest, got shots of a huge rat snake leaving the nest with food bulges up and down its body. Western rat snake.  C'est la vie.  Seems like that was a couple of weeks after these shots.

description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
Photo 1:
Odd Wood Duck
Wood ducks look strange when they change from their pretty breeding colors into their drab summer (eclipse) colors.  But this duck is stranger still.  It has both male & female characteristics.  Not a juvenile, they have dull olive color bills.  Male traits here are that colorful bill that remains even in summer and the colorful head crest feathers.  Female traits are the brown eye instead of red, the shape of the white outlining the eye and the lack of a white chin strap going up the neck. Males keep the red eyes and white chin strap even in the summer.
Photo 2:
Another View Of The Odd Wood Duck
From every angle and when I lightened up colors all the way on the desktop briefly, that eye stayed brown.  Pretty cool.  
Photo 3:
Comparison shot of mine that shows 1 male & 2 female wood ducks in eclipse colors.  Male eyes red, female eyes brown.  male no white around eye and white chin strip and colorful bill.  females white around eye, no chin strap and non colorful bill.
So, is this a gynandromorph or am I missing something?

Intersex Duck
Saw the peculiar wood duck again but this time I know what I'm looking at since I researched it last time.  She is an intersex duck with colors and plumage of both male and female.  Brown eye, white eye ring and lack of chin strap are female markings while colorful beak and colorful head crest is like a male.  I found out that in birds, the chromosomal sex-determination is reversed, making the default development male. When estrogen levels are suppressed with age, that default shows up, since they're growing in their feathers every year.  Apparently that works for beak color too.

description:
Video of calling:
https://youtu.be/6ALlUShipFA
Surprisingly, this spectacular male Wood Duck was difficult to spot.  It seems remarkably shy and chose to remain hidden, except for this brief glimpse as it headed behind the reeds.

Wood Ducks don't bring any nesting material into the nest box, so the box is charged with 5-6" of Aspen wood shavings. Initially the hen laying one egg a day will bury her eggs in the shavings. When the hen nears the completion of her clutch of eggs, she will pull down from her breast to make a blanket of down mixed with shavings to cover her eggs.

The first attached photo taken inside the nest box shows a mound of shavings mixed with down--a sure sign that eggs have been buried. The second photo shows 7 eggs which were uncovered and re-covered after the photo was taken.

In my experience the most eggs that were laid in a nest box by a single hen was 14. All 14 eggs  hatched and 14 ducklings fledged.

---
📸: By Lee Pauser

This observation was part of a nest box trail done in conjunction with the California Bluebird Recovery Program (CBRP), which runs the Cavity Nesters Recovery Program (CNRP). CNRP involves many volunteers across California who establish and monitor nest box trails for cavity-nesting birds. During the breeding season, these boxes are checked weekly for parasitism, predation, number of eggs, nestlings, and number of young fledged. Then at the end of the nesting season, volunteers submit their results to CBRP. We compile these results and submit them to the Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s NestWatch program and other interested organizations.

description:
Wood Ducks don't bring any nesting material into the nest box, so the box is charged with 5-6" of Aspen wood shavings. Initially the hen laying one egg a day will bury her eggs in the shavings. The first attached photo taken inside the nest box shows a mound of shavings--a sure sign that eggs have been buried. The second photo shows 4 eggs which were uncovered, counted and re-covered after the photo was taken.

When the hen nears the completion of her clutch of eggs, she will pull down from her breast to make a blanket of down mixed with shavings to cover her eggs while she is out of the box.

---
📸: By Lee Pauser

This observation was part of a nest box trail done in conjunction with the California Bluebird Recovery Program (CBRP), which runs the Cavity Nesters Recovery Program (CNRP). CNRP involves many volunteers across California who establish and monitor nest box trails for cavity-nesting birds. During the breeding season, these boxes are checked weekly for parasitism, predation, number of eggs, nestlings, and number of young fledged. Then at the end of the nesting season, volunteers submit their results to CBRP. We compile these results and submit them to the Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s NestWatch program and other interested organizations.
